271	
272	When: a plain screenhack makes two pixmaps, draws into them and `XCopyArea`s the
273	result to the window (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes, Halftone,
274	Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole). Since #61 this works as copied, but a back
275	buffer costs 434 KB of PSRAM and a full-frame copy each frame, and dirties
276	every row, so the push loses what the dirty rectangle (#52) saves. Draw
277	straight on the canvas instead, as below. (These eight were ported before #61,
278	when the copy from a blank pixmap erased the picture.)
279	
280	- A pinned hash of a blank frame passes silently (`0xa4f79500bd791711ull`, which
281	  is also Pedal's at frame 200). Look at the frame before pinning.
282	- Upstream switches the buffering off under `HAVE_JWXYZ` ("Don't second-guess
283	  Quartz's double-buffering"), or reads a `doubleBuffer` resource. Write
284	  `hacks/<name>_direct.c`: include `screenhack.h` and the math headers, empty
285	  `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`, `#define HAVE_JWXYZ`, include the unmodified hack and
286	  register its `HackEntry`. Exclude the original from `build_src_filter` in all
287	  three environments. `grep HAVE_JWXYZ` first: Interaggregate also uses it for
288	  pixel packing, but only in the 24 and 32 bit cases, and the canvas is 16 bit.
289	- A hack that uses a pixmap as storage needs no wrapper. Truchet draws a canvas
290	  bigger than the window into an 866 by 866 pixmap (1.5 MB of PSRAM) and
291	  scrolls it with `XCopyArea` offsets.
292	
293	## Restart leak test
294	
295	When: the hack restarts itself. Override its cycle resource in the test (for
296	example `*maxCycles: 3`), compare `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()`
297	before and after many restarts, and prove the test sees a leak by removing a
298	`free` in a temporary copy or leaking from a shim function. Never leave the
299	hack changed: `cmp` it afterwards.
300	
301	Measure the growth first, then set the tolerance just above it (Pacman: exactly
302	0, so 512 bytes). A loose one passes a leaked GC; mutation-check by leaking one.
303	
304	On the device, work out how long a restart takes: cycles times the frame time.
305	Substrate's 10,000 cycles at about 160 ms is 27 minutes, and the restart showed
306	at about 25. Capture that long, with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`.
307	
308	## Stopping before the first draw
309	
310	When: the hack allocates on its first `draw` (look for a lazy `initted` flag)
311	but sizes its `free` from values set in `init`. Two quick button presses, or a
312	press with the 90 s rotation, free a hack before it has drawn once. Blaster
313	sets `NUM_ROBOTS` in init, allocates `robots` in draw, and its free loops over
314	`robots[i].lasers`, so freeing it first dereferenced NULL. The dump tool with 0
315	frames exited 139.
316	
317	- `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame` starts and stops every
318	  hack with no frame, so a new port that has this problem fails the host suite.
319	- To fix it without editing the hack, write a wrapper that includes the
320	  unmodified source with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers the hack
321	  itself, with a `free` that makes the loop safe (`hacks/blaster_safe.c`).
322	- A real press is rarely handled in that window: Rod's presses on the device
323	  all landed after the first step. Rely on the test, not on pressing buttons.
324	- An xlockmore hack cannot be re-registered that way: `xlockmore.h` has no
325	  include guard, so the hack's own include redefines `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`
326	  after the wrapper empties it. Swap the callback in the table instead, from a
327	  constructor: `<name>_xlockmore_function_table.hack_init = my_init;`
328	  (`loop_direct.c`, `hypnowheel_single_gl.c`).
329	
330	## Tests that cannot be fooled
331	
332	A test that runs a real hack can pass for the wrong reason. Pyro clears its own
333	window in `init`, so a "starts black" test through Pyro passed with the runner
334	deliberately broken. Test shared runner behaviour with stub hacks
335	(`test_runner_xsft.c`) and mutate the code to see the test fail.
336	
337	A check can also be true before the hack has run. "At least 20 non-black
338	pixels" proved a hack drew, until Substrate started on a white canvas and
339	passed without drawing at all. Compare with the canvas as the hack started, and
340	keep a stub hack that draws nothing, on the colour that fooled the old check, to
341	show the test can fail. When a change alters what every hack starts with (the
342	background colour, an initial canvas), re-read the older tests that assume the
343	old start.
344	
345	A bounds guard can be unreachable through the public API. TinyGL's clipper
346	keeps a line inside the view volume and its viewport maps that to at most pixel
347	63.5, so two of the four guards in the smooth-line plot survived mutation until
348	a test used a viewport bigger than the canvas. Mutate each guard on its own
349	(a scratchpad script that edits, runs the suite and restores in `finally`),
350	and when one survives, find an input that reaches it or say it is defensive.
351	Wrapping bugs can also hide in what is stored, not what is drawn: a depth that
352	wrapped round only showed when a third fill was drawn afterwards.
353	
354	## Background colour
355	
356	The runner paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before `init`,
357	as `screenhack.c` paints the window. Substrate (`.background: white`) depends
358	on it. Every earlier hack asks for black or nothing.
359	
360	## Skipping a hack
361	
362	Threads, GL, Xft and shared memory are not worth porting. Record the name and
363	the reason in `tools/failed_ports.txt` (`name: reason`); the scorer marks it as
364	abandoned.
365	
366	## Worktree setup
367	
368	A fresh worktree lacks the ignored `vendor/`, `.venv/` and `.platformio/`:
369	symlink them from the main checkout. They show as untracked, so `git add`
370	named paths, never `-A`. Adding them to `.git/info/exclude` changes state shared
371	with every worktree: ask Rod first.
372	
373	A worktree session refuses `source`, `$VAR` in a command and `&&` chains with a
374	computed path. Run plain commands with literal paths, for example
375	`PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<worktree>/.platformio ../.venv/bin/pio test -e native`.
376	
377	## Device capture
378	
379	- Pin the hack with `-DSTART_HACK=\"name\"` and add `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`, or the
380	  board rotates to the next hack after 90 s.
381	- Send upload output to a file, never through `head`, and look for "Hash of
382	  data verified".
383	- Capture 150 s or more of serial in the background, longer to see a restart.
384	  Read `step`, `push`, `wait`, heap and PSRAM, and any "Stack canary".
385	- Compare with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: pushes became
386	  41-45 ms on every hack after the byte-order fix, against 31 ms before (#23).
387	- Pinning a frame hash: set the new hack's `kBaseline` entry to `1`, run
388	  `pio test -f test_hacks`, read `Was N` in the failure and convert with
389	  `python3 -c "print('0x%016xull' % N)"`. Pin only after looking at the frame
390	  (and never type the hex by hand: one was wrong).
391	- Showing Rod a hack: flash `-DSTART_HACK=\"first\" -DROTATE_SECONDS=25` with
392	  `XS_LOGO=...` so the new ones come up in order, then tell him which, and that
393	  the button steps backwards (from Pyro it wraps to the last hack).

# Adding a hack

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md. The order of work is in `SKILL.md`.

The `port-hack` skill orders this work, says what to read for before copying a
hack, and holds a recipe per trap. The steps:

1. Check its row in `docs/porting-assessment.md` (effort and Speed band) and
   read its licence header.
2. Update the expected list in `firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c` and see
   it fail.
3. Copy the file to `firmware/src/hacks/<name>/<name>.c`, add the notices row
   and an `extern` plus entry in `hacks/registry.c`.
4. Fill shim gaps test-first in `firmware/test/test_xshim/`. The compile
   check in `score_hacks.py` shows what is missing.
5. Host tests pass, dump a frame and look at it, then (with Rod's go-ahead)
   flash and measure fps and free heap/PSRAM over serial. To pin its frame
   hash after looking at the frame, put `0x1ull` in `kBaseline`, run
   `pio test -e native -f test_hacks`, convert the "Was N" in the failure line
   with `python3 -c "print(hex(N))"`, and run it again.
6. Regenerate the assessment and add measurements to
   `tools/assessment_measured.md`, then re-run the speed backtest: each port
   adds a point to the check of the Speed bands, which were fitted to the first
   29 hacks. To make a port a real test, commit its host time and predicted
   range first (`docs/speed-predictions.md` shows the form), flash it as copied,
   and add its name to `HOLDOUT` in `tools/speed_backtest.py`. The first four
   (Mountain, Epicycle, Kaleidescope, Celtic) all fell where predicted.
7. If a hack is slow and `double`-heavy (many `double`s, `sqrt`, `sin`/`cos`,
   `pow`), try a single-precision wrapper like `hacks/galaxy_single.c` (for a
   plain screenhack, `hacks/substrate_single.c`; the recipe is in the skill's
   `techniques.md`), and compare double and float frames at several frame
   counts. A resource
   override can skip a hack's restart cleanup: Galaxy leaked at `count: 2`, so
   leak-test any override.
8. If Rod drops a port after seeing it (Hypnowheel, Boing; Celtic was dropped
   and came back through issue #37): remove it
   from `g_hacks[]`, the expected list, its hash and its leak test; keep the
   source and notices row; add `name: reason` (short: it is printed as a
   bullet) to `tools/failed_ports.txt`. For a GL hack, keep the `<name>_gl.c`
   wrapper but exclude it and the directory (`-<hacks/boing/>
   -<hacks/boing_gl.c>`) in all three `build_src_filter` lines, or it still
   builds. A reason Rod gave in his own words ("boring on a small screen") is
   the reason to record. File an issue only if there is something to come back
   to.
# Porting techniques

Recipes for the traps listed in `SKILL.md`. Each says when it applies, what to
do, and what it did the last time.

## Build-time patch

When: the hack's own constants make it too big for the board. Maze keeps a
1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one `calloc`, about
20 MB, and the board has 8 MB of PSRAM.

- The copy in `hacks/<name>/` stays byte-identical to upstream (`cmp` it).
- A PlatformIO `pre:` script (`firmware/patch_maze.py`) writes a patched copy
  into the build directory, using a tested function (`tools/maze_patch.py`)
  that raises if upstream's lines change. A wrapper (`hacks/maze_small.c`)
  includes that copy, and the original is excluded in `build_src_filter` of
  all three environments (`stopwatch`, `native`, `dump`).
- Maze's limits went from 1000 to 80: about 125 KB.
- A patch can switch off a branch (Pacman's `NRAND (2) == 0` becomes `0`) or
  replace a whole function (its route search becomes a loop). Check the
  original's SHA-256 so an upstream edit fails the build. Before a rewrite, pin
  a long-run fingerprint taken with the original (30,000 frames, every ghost's
  position every 100), show the code ran, and mutate the order to watch the pin
  fail.

## Single precision

When: a hot loop does `double` maths or calls `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt` or `pow`.
The ESP32-S3 has a single-precision FPU only, so double runs in software.

- Find the hot loop first and count the calls. Substrate makes four `sin` calls
  per sand grain, with 64 grains a crack and up to 100 cracks: about 25,000
  software `sin`s a frame. Its step grew from 5 ms to 121 ms as the picture
  filled.
- Wrapper `hacks/<name>_single.c`: include the framework headers first, then
  `hacks/single_precision.h`, then the unmodified hack. Exclude the original in
  `build_src_filter` of all three environments.
- `M_PI` is a double literal, so the angle arithmetic stays double: put
  `#undef M_PI` and a float definition after the header. Literals such as
  `0.81` stay double too, and a header cannot change them: `0.5 * x` with a
  float `x` is software double maths. Check the wrapper's object for soft-double
  helpers with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm braid.o | grep ' U __.*df'` (compile with
  `-Os -mlongcalls` and the shim's include paths). If any remain, rewrite the
  literals at build time as Braid does: `tools/float_literals.py` (tested, skips
  strings and comments) run by `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`, and the
  wrapper includes `<name>_floatlit.c` from the build directory. GCC's
  `-fsingle-precision-constant` does the same, but Apple clang ignores it, so
  host tests would run other arithmetic than the board.
- Galaxy, Drift, Discrete, Flame and Substrate were wrapped before this check
  and have not been looked at for double literals.
- Hand-written `sin` and `cos` (`hacks/fast_trig.h`) moved Braid by 5%. Do the
  literals first.
- Compare double and float frames at several counts. Early frames match; a
  chaotic hack diverges later but should keep its look.
- GL hacks too: Hypnowheel's spiral called `cos` and `sin` in `double` for
  every vertex, about 275 ms of a 706 ms step, hidden behind a fill-heavy look.
  Its wrapper (`hypnowheel_single_gl.c`) adapts `get_position` and
  `get_rotation` as HexTrail's does.
- Results: Galaxy 5 to 14 fps. Substrate step 119-121 ms to 37-38 ms, 6.2 to
  12.5 fps.
- A hack that passes the address of its own `double` local to a shim function
  (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &s, &v)`) writes eight bytes into a four-byte float, and
  the compiler does not warn. Moire's frames were all different from the
  double build's until `moire_single.c` mapped the call to an adapter defined
  before `single_precision.h`. Cmp the wrapper's frames against the unmodified
  hack's. A hack with no decimal literals must stay out of
  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses it.
- Once the maths is float, look at the fills before the next idea. CWaves'
  cosines were 4 ms of a 61 ms step; its 233 column fills were 57 (a thin
  full-height rectangle touches a new cache line a store). See `hacks.md`.
- A float build can break a check that held in double. Both the S3 (`madd.s`)
  and arm64 fuse a multiply and an add, so `t*n - floor(t*n)` uses the exact
  product for the subtraction and the rounded one for the `floor`, and can
  come out slightly negative: Celtic's `assert(tt>=0 && tt<1)` aborted at
  t 0.331093 with 3422 segments. The 3000-frame test (`pio test`) found it
  on the host, and the same abort would have hit the board. Compute the
  product once in a build-time patch (`tools/celtic_patch.py`). Map any libm
  call the hack makes that `single_precision.h` does not (`rint`, `floor`),
  and check the object with `nm` for `__*df*` helpers, not only `__muldf3`.

## Slow hack

When: a ported hack runs under about 10 fps and the push is not the cause
(`step` in the serial line is large).

- For a GL hack, flash a `-DGL_PROFILE` build first (AGENTS.md): it splits
  the frame into stages, and time in none of them is the hack's own code.
  Issue #73 guessed Hypnowheel was 70 percent blended fill; the profile showed
  a third of its frame was `double` trig.
- A worst-case microbenchmark is not the workload. A PSRAM cache miss costs
  about 220 cycles, which suggested GL fill was memory-bound; a banded renderer
  in internal RAM, built on that, was exact and slower (neighbouring triangles
  share cache lines). A/B the first working slice of a speed idea on the board
  before building the rest, and stop if it does not pay.
- Do not trust a host profile (`sample` on the dump program) for where the
  time goes. A Mac does `double` at full speed, so software-double code looks
  cheap there: Braid's disc fill was 6% on the host and the largest cost on the
  board.
- Split the step on the device with a temporary build flag that makes the
  expensive call return at once (Braid: `XDrawLine`). The step left is the
  hack's own cost; the difference is the drawing. Remove the flag before
  committing.
- Count what is called per frame (segments, calls, rows) before guessing,
  and look at the object file for soft-double helpers (see "Single precision").
- Change one thing, pin that the pixels did not move (`cmp` frames at several
  counts, or the pinned hash), flash, and compare second windows. Braid's four
  changes were worth 2.7-3.2 times, 1.05, and 1.3.
- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1) are the costly path: a quad filled a row at
  a time, plus two discs for round caps. `stroke.c` keeps a table of disc rows
  by width up to 16. A wide full circle through `XDrawArc` is about a thousand
  such segments (Deluxe: 94% of a frame, 2-5 fps); `stroke_circle` fills it as
  a ring in two spans a row.
- When the cost is overpaint, not `double` maths, a host split does find the
  dominant call: `#define XDrawArc(...) 0` in the wrapper, `pio run -e dump`,
  then `/usr/bin/time -p .pio/build/dump/program <index> 400 out.raw` three
  times, against the baseline. It cannot see costs that live in memory
  traffic (Deluxe's alpha mask: nothing on the host, 3-5 ms on the board).
- Counting works where timing misleads: a scratch copy of the hack with a
  counter in the inner function and a macro round `XDrawLine` gave Celtic's
  spline evaluations and line draws per draw call on the host, by graph type.
  A cost per eval and per line fitted to a first device capture (about 1.7 us
  and 22 us, from three graph types and a handful of windows) estimated 63 ms
  for the biggest type after the change; the next capture's 12.6-76.8 ms did
  not contradict it, but the log does not say which type each window was, so
  the fit is unchecked.
- A hack's own pacing constants can be the lever: Celtic's 0.0001 tick (a
  patch scales it, `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE`) set both the look-ahead's work and how
  many draw calls a picture takes. Count the draw calls a picture takes and
  the pause after it before reading `fps=`: with a 5 s pause the column read
  5.2 in every window and measured the pause, not the drawing. Use
  `1000 / (step + push + delay)` for the drawing rate.
- Heap and speed were two problems in Celtic and one fix cured only the
  first: the graph sized to the screen cut a pattern's heap about 9 times and
  left spline evaluations per call unchanged. Measure both after each change.
- A hack that redraws its whole picture every frame to animate colour (Braid)
  costs its full draw each frame whatever the push does. Check this before
  porting; the scorer does not flag it yet.
- A fix that moves the frame rate by under 5% shows the maths was not the
  cost. HexTrail in single precision went from 12.7 to 13.0 fps; the 2.3 fps
  that mattered came from reading what the GL layer does each frame
  (`glshim_clear`) and finding a depth clear that nothing read, because the hack
  never enables the depth test. Run `nm` on the object, then read the shared
  code the hack calls before trying a third idea in the hack.
- A step that grows over the hack's cycle (HexTrail: 19 ms to a ceiling, then it
  restarts) needs the worst window, not the mean. Capture at least one full
  cycle (150 s covered HexTrail's 65 s), read the lowest `fps=`, and compare the
  time spent below 10 fps with the rotation interval: Rod saw it fall under 10
  before the 25 s change. If a resource such as `count` scales the cost, give it
  an `#ifndef` default in `registry.c` (`HEXTRAIL_COUNT`) so one flash tests
  another value, and measure two or three values: count 6 gave a mean of 12.7,
  10 gave 9.1 and 20 gave 5.7, in double precision.

## Thin lines in a GL hack

When: a GL hack draws hairlines or fades (Unknown Pleasures) and looks right
in a host frame but flickers on the board. Work down this list, one layer at a
time, and look at the screen (or film) after each; each layer hid the next.

- Lines hop. TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel, so a drifting line
  jumps. `tinygl_patch.py` keeps the fractional position and draws a Wu line
  when the hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Triangles are still snapped.
- Quads that hide the lines behind them hide nothing, or the picture is
  speckled grey. TinyGL's blend adds colours, ignores alpha and misreads our
  byte-swapped pixels, so `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA` is drawn as an
  opaque fill. Smooth lines carry no alpha, so a hack's per-line fade is lost.
- A line drawn on its own polygon's edge is erased in dashes: `glPolygonOffset`
  was stored and never read. The patch applies it, plus a margin for the
  vertex snapping. Check the effect on the host by the second difference of a
  frame's total brightness while the picture drifts a fraction of a pixel; change
  one thing at a time, because blending once made the experiment unable to
  show any effect.
- Pieces of a line vanish for one refresh. The panel scans while the push
  writes, so a seam crosses the picture. Set `sync_to_refresh` on the hack
  (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`); see `.claude/rules/device-display.md` for the
  offset, why it is only valid for a full-frame push, and how to film the
  result. Cost: up to a refresh of latency a frame, so only a hack that needs
  it should ask.
- Budget with `gl_budget.py` but expect it to be off: it has no blend term
  (Unknown Pleasures was predicted at 251 ms and ran at 267, then 197 once the
  fills were opaque). Add the measured row as a calibration point.
- After all that a dimming of about 14% for 25 ms at each push remained (issue
  #68). Do not promise a hack is flicker-free from a host frame or from the
  absence of vanishing lines alone.

## Stack check

When: locals over a few KB. Compile the hack with `-O1 -fstack-usage` (flags in
AGENTS.md) and keep each frame well under the 16 KB loop stack. Host tests
cannot see an overflow: Rorschach's 9.6 KB array rebooted the device on its
first frame, and only the serial log's "Stack canary" showed it.

Recursion: replay it, don't guess. Run the hack on a pthread with a painted
1 MB stack over several seeds and thousands of frames (Pacman's generator: 236
KB median, 315 KB worst; `ulimit -s` saw only the first, shallow level). Read a
frame's size from the ELF (`xtensa-esp32s3-elf-objdump -d`, `entry a1, N`), and
decode a panic backtrace with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-addr2line` against an ELF
rebuilt with the same flags. A recursion over a grid is bounded by its cells:
replay it from every start.

## Large allocations

When: one allocation of 100 KB or more, or the hack calls `exit()` if it fails.

- `unsigned long` is 4 bytes on the device and 8 on the host, so host leak
  numbers are double the device's.
- Plain `malloc` and `realloc` of two 868 KB buffers (Substrate) landed in
  PSRAM: free PSRAM fell by 1,742,096 bytes, which is 2 x 466 x 466 x 4 plus a
  few KB. Internal heap barely moved.
- On restart the buffers were freed and allocated again, and free PSRAM
  returned to the same value. Read heap and PSRAM in the log to confirm this
  for each large hack.

## Images

Colour pixmaps are canvases: every drawing primitive, `XCopyArea` and
`XCopyPlane` draw into them. Bitmaps take only `XCopyArea` from another
bitmap. There is no PNG
decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads a raw RGB565 blob and
mask (format in `ximage-loader.h`), made by `tools/make_logo_blob.py`.
`XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repository root) swaps the logo for a local
image at build time. Keep a third-party logo under `vendor/`, out of git.

A big blob (Pacman's is 3 MB as C text) is built from `vendor/` by a `pre:`
script and never committed; write it to a `.partial` file and rename it.

## Pixmap double buffering

When: a plain screenhack makes two pixmaps, draws into them and `XCopyArea`s the
result to the window (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes, Halftone,
Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole). Since #61 this works as copied, but a back
buffer costs 434 KB of PSRAM and a full-frame copy each frame, and dirties
every row, so the push loses what the dirty rectangle (#52) saves. Draw
straight on the canvas instead, as below. (These eight were ported before #61,
when the copy from a blank pixmap erased the picture.)

- A pinned hash of a blank frame passes silently (`0xa4f79500bd791711ull`, which
  is also Pedal's at frame 200). Look at the frame before pinning.
- Upstream switches the buffering off under `HAVE_JWXYZ` ("Don't second-guess
  Quartz's double-buffering"), or reads a `doubleBuffer` resource. Write
  `hacks/<name>_direct.c`: include `screenhack.h` and the math headers, empty
  `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`, `#define HAVE_JWXYZ`, include the unmodified hack and
  register its `HackEntry`. Exclude the original from `build_src_filter` in all
  three environments. `grep HAVE_JWXYZ` first: Interaggregate also uses it for
  pixel packing, but only in the 24 and 32 bit cases, and the canvas is 16 bit.
- A hack that uses a pixmap as storage needs no wrapper. Truchet draws a canvas
  bigger than the window into an 866 by 866 pixmap (1.5 MB of PSRAM) and
  scrolls it with `XCopyArea` offsets.

## Restart leak test

When: the hack restarts itself. Override its cycle resource in the test (for
example `*maxCycles: 3`), compare `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()`
before and after many restarts, and prove the test sees a leak by removing a
`free` in a temporary copy or leaking from a shim function. Never leave the
hack changed: `cmp` it afterwards.

Measure the growth first, then set the tolerance just above it (Pacman: exactly
0, so 512 bytes). A loose one passes a leaked GC; mutation-check by leaking one.

On the device, work out how long a restart takes: cycles times the frame time.
Substrate's 10,000 cycles at about 160 ms is 27 minutes, and the restart showed
at about 25. Capture that long, with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`.

## Stopping before the first draw

When: the hack allocates on its first `draw` (look for a lazy `initted` flag)
but sizes its `free` from values set in `init`. Two quick button presses, or a
press with the 90 s rotation, free a hack before it has drawn once. Blaster
sets `NUM_ROBOTS` in init, allocates `robots` in draw, and its free loops over
`robots[i].lasers`, so freeing it first dereferenced NULL. The dump tool with 0
frames exited 139.

- `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame` starts and stops every
  hack with no frame, so a new port that has this problem fails the host suite.
- To fix it without editing the hack, write a wrapper that includes the
  unmodified source with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers the hack
  itself, with a `free` that makes the loop safe (`hacks/blaster_safe.c`).
- A real press is rarely handled in that window: Rod's presses on the device
  all landed after the first step. Rely on the test, not on pressing buttons.
- An xlockmore hack cannot be re-registered that way: `xlockmore.h` has no
  include guard, so the hack's own include redefines `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`
  after the wrapper empties it. Swap the callback in the table instead, from a
  constructor: `<name>_xlockmore_function_table.hack_init = my_init;`
  (`loop_direct.c`, `hypnowheel_single_gl.c`).

## Tests that cannot be fooled

A test that runs a real hack can pass for the wrong reason. Pyro clears its own
window in `init`, so a "starts black" test through Pyro passed with the runner
deliberately broken. Test shared runner behaviour with stub hacks
(`test_runner_xsft.c`) and mutate the code to see the test fail.

A check can also be true before the hack has run. "At least 20 non-black
pixels" proved a hack drew, until Substrate started on a white canvas and
passed without drawing at all. Compare with the canvas as the hack started, and
keep a stub hack that draws nothing, on the colour that fooled the old check, to
show the test can fail. When a change alters what every hack starts with (the
background colour, an initial canvas), re-read the older tests that assume the
old start.

A bounds guard can be unreachable through the public API. TinyGL's clipper
keeps a line inside the view volume and its viewport maps that to at most pixel
63.5, so two of the four guards in the smooth-line plot survived mutation until
a test used a viewport bigger than the canvas. Mutate each guard on its own
(a scratchpad script that edits, runs the suite and restores in `finally`),
and when one survives, find an input that reaches it or say it is defensive.
Wrapping bugs can also hide in what is stored, not what is drawn: a depth that
wrapped round only showed when a third fill was drawn afterwards.

## Background colour

The runner paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before `init`,
as `screenhack.c` paints the window. Substrate (`.background: white`) depends
on it. Every earlier hack asks for black or nothing.

## Skipping a hack

Threads, GL, Xft and shared memory are not worth porting. Record the name and
the reason in `tools/failed_ports.txt` (`name: reason`); the scorer marks it as
abandoned.

## Worktree setup

A fresh worktree lacks the ignored `vendor/`, `.venv/` and `.platformio/`:
symlink them from the main checkout. They show as untracked, so `git add`
named paths, never `-A`. Adding them to `.git/info/exclude` changes state shared
with every worktree: ask Rod first.

A worktree session refuses `source`, `$VAR` in a command and `&&` chains with a
computed path. Run plain commands with literal paths, for example
`PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<worktree>/.platformio ../.venv/bin/pio test -e native`.

## Device capture

- Pin the hack with `-DSTART_HACK=\"name\"` and add `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`, or the
  board rotates to the next hack after 90 s.
- Send upload output to a file, never through `head`, and look for "Hash of
  data verified".
- Capture 150 s or more of serial in the background, longer to see a restart.
  Read `step`, `push`, `wait`, heap and PSRAM, and any "Stack canary".
- Compare with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: pushes became
  41-45 ms on every hack after the byte-order fix, against 31 ms before (#23).
- Pinning a frame hash: set the new hack's `kBaseline` entry to `1`, run
  `pio test -f test_hacks`, read `Was N` in the failure and convert with
  `python3 -c "print('0x%016xull' % N)"`. Pin only after looking at the frame
  (and never type the hex by hand: one was wrong).
- Showing Rod a hack: flash `-DSTART_HACK=\"first\" -DROTATE_SECONDS=25` with
  `XS_LOGO=...` so the new ones come up in order, then tell him which, and that
  the button steps backwards (from Pyro it wraps to the last hack).

# Porting assessment

Rough effort to port each xscreensaver hack to the StopWatch X11 shim,
generated from xscreensaver 6.16 by `tools/score_hacks.py`. Regenerate
it with `uv run tools/score_hacks.py`.

## How to read this

- **283 hacks** were scanned: every `hacks/*.c` and `hacks/glx/*.c`
  that registers itself with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`. Another 125
  files (3D models, helper libraries, command-line tools) are excluded and
  listed at the end.
- The scan is static and heuristic. For each 2D hack it counts the Xlib
  calls in the source that the shim does not declare, and it also
  syntax-checks the unmodified source against the shim's headers
  (`cc -fsyntax-only`). Anything the compiler cannot find is a **shim
  gap**: a missing header, type, struct field, constant or function.
  That second check catches helpers hacks reach through `utils/` that a
  count of Xlib calls cannot see. The effort rating does not run anything,
  so treat it as a prioritisation aid, not an estimate. It also says nothing
  about speed: see "Speed" below.
- The **All hacks** table lists the work still to do first, from least to
  most effort (S, M, L, XL) and then by name, and the ported hacks last.
  Its **Ported** column shows ✅ for a hack in the
  firmware's registry (`hacks/registry.c`) and ❌ for one that was
  attempted and abandoned (see "Failed ports" after the table, which only
  appears when there are any). Failures are recorded in
  `tools/failed_ports.txt`.

## Effort ratings

| --- | --- | --- |

State at the end of the 2026-10-11 GL speed session. `main` is at `12a130b` (PR #79 and #81 merged, plus the lessons commit). The badge text defaults to "Rod"; **use the default name**.

**The board is not on a `main` build.** At the end of the #77 session (2026-10-11) it held a `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` HexTrail build from `feature/77-round-screen-corners` (PR #85), pinned with rotation off. Rod then handed the board to another session ("I'll let the other session drive it"). Do not flash or open the serial port without his explicit approval each time: [[feedback-flash-only-with-explicit-approval]].

Open tickets (gh issue list, end of 2026-10-11): #31 #32 #37 #44 (Pipes: Rod's decisions in his 2026-10-11 comment, see [[project-gl-speed-overnight-43-44]]) #46 #54 #56 #57 #59 #65 #68 #70 #71 #73 (Hypnowheel, out at 4.0 fps) #74 #75 #77 #80 (draw GL_LINE_LOOP/GL_POLYGON? The badge adds about 16 to 20 ms to `push=`; read `push=` from the second 5 s window (the first includes the overlay stamp). With the dirty rectangle a GL hack's push is 2 to 14 ms and `rows=` is well under 466.

Rod said on 2026-10-11, after #77's eye checks: "PLEASE STOP FLASHING THE DEVICE unless I give you an approval. I'll let the other session drive it for now."

Earlier in that session he had given blanket permission to flash for the task. I had then flashed the board once more when he asked for the comparison build, and he wanted it back for another session.

**Why:** several sessions share one board, and an unexpected flash wipes another session's run. A task-wide go-ahead ends when Rod says so, or when the eye checks he asked for are done.

Merged to main as PR #83 (merge commit 486098e) on 2026-10-11; branch and worktree removed, main fast-forwarded. Open follow-ups: #82 (memcpy rows in XPutImage; 2× is blit-bound at ~21.5 fps, 1× 28.9) and #84 (play the original flap soundtrack on the ES8311 speaker; labels enhancement + hack).

Rod's decisions: name `ad-flyingtoasters`; 2× chunky pixels, 6 flyers, by default after seeing both on the device (1× via `-DAD_TOASTERS_SCALE=1`, 10 flyers); random 1-bit/colour and doneness per start — he loves the 1-bit art. The board was last flashed with a pinned 2× build, rotation off.

**Why:** Berkeley Systems art can't go in the public MIT repo, so art is extracted at build time from git-ignored `vendor/after-dark-v2.0v-800k` (ScummVM model; disk also on archive.org/details/after-dark-2.0v-800k). `check_notices.py` lists `hacks/ad_flyingtoasters/` in OWN_HACK_DIRS; `score_hacks.py` lists it in OWN_HACKS.

"""Copies an xscreensaver hack into the firmware and registers it.

    uv run tools/wire_hack.py <name> <Class> "<copyright text>" \\
        [--notice "<licence column>"] [--xlockmore] [--glx]

Does the mechanical steps of `.claude/skills/port-hack/adding-a-hack.md`
(steps 2 and 3): copies `vendor/xscreensaver-6.16/hacks/<name>.c` to
`firmware/src/hacks/<name>/`, adds the registry entry (last in the button
order), the name to the expected list in `test_hacks.c`, a frame hash of `0`
(skipped until pinned: see "Batches" in that skill), a leak test, and the
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md row. It does not touch `platformio.ini`, write a
wrapper, or fill a shim gap. Read the hack's licence first.

--xlockmore registers with `XLOCKMORE_HACK(name, "Class")`, for a hack built on
xlockmore.h (it has `MI_DISPLAY`); otherwise it expects the hack to define its
own `<name>_hack` through XSCREENSAVER_MODULE.
"""

import argparse
import re
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
UPSTREAM = "vendor/xscreensaver-6.16"


def _insert_before(text: str, marker: str, addition: str) -> str:
    i = text.find(marker)
    if i < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"cannot find `{marker}`")
    return text[:i] + addition + text[i:]


def wire(
    root: Path,
    name: str,
    cls: str,
    copyright_text: str,
    notice: str = "jwz permission notice (above)",
    xlockmore: bool = False,
    glx: bool = False,
) -> None:
    src = root / UPSTREAM / "hacks" / ("glx" if glx else "") / f"{name}.c"
    if not src.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(src)
    dst = root / "firmware" / "src" / "hacks" / name / f"{name}.c"
    registry = root / "firmware" / "src" / "hacks" / "registry.c"
    tests = root / "firmware" / "test" / "test_hacks" / "test_hacks.c"
    notices = root / "THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md"

    reg = registry.read_text()
    if re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(name)}_hack\b", reg):
        raise ValueError(f"{name} is already in registry.c")
    if xlockmore:
        decl = f'XLOCKMORE_HACK({name}, "{cls}");\n'
    else:
        decl = f"extern const HackEntry {name}_hack;\n"
    reg = _insert_before(reg, "const HackEntry *const g_hacks[]", decl + "\n")
    reg, n = re.subn(
        r"    &(\w+)_hack\};", rf"    &\1_hack,\n    &{name}_hack}};", reg, count=1
    )
    if n != 1:
        raise ValueError("cannot find the end of g_hacks[]")

    t = tests.read_text()
    t, n = re.subn(
        r'"\};\n  const int n = sizeof\(expected\)',
        f'",\n                                         "{cls}"}};\n  const int n = sizeof(expected)',
        t,
        count=1,
    )
    if n != 1:
        raise ValueError("cannot find the expected list in test_hacks.c")
    t, n = re.subn(
        r"(\};\n\nvoid test_frames_of_every_hack_but_maze_match_main)",
        f"    0, /* {cls}: not yet pinned */\n\\1",
        t,
        count=1,
tools/env.sh
tools/flash_and_capture.sh

  `random()` always starts the same one: force another with a temporary
  `*mode:` override to measure it. Rotation reaches other modes because the

  doubled) saturated, so the screen was white. `tools/fireworkx_patch.py`

  freed its cells and drew nothing more (a black screen at 18 fps, half the

  `failed_ports.txt` entry stay). `hypnowheel_single_gl.c` registers it only
  with `-DHYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`, as the last entry, for measuring. A board profile

  fill as first thought; single precision gives 2.2 fps. The rest is fill
  (about 334 ms): `-DHYPNOWHEEL_HALF` renders at half resolution

  every store lands on a different cache line of the PSRAM canvas: after single
  precision took the step from 95 to 61 ms, 57 of those were the fills and 4

  full-height column into canvas row 0 and the draw wrapper copies that row

  compiler warning. `moire_single.c` defines an adapter before

  the adapter was in. A hack with no decimal literals (Moire) must not be in

  `DO_STIPPLE` block that is never defined.

  and the expansion were 26 and 27 ms, because 64-bit index maths is several
  instructions an operation on a 32-bit core and the expansion branched on
  every pixel. After clipping everything fits an int; a byte table of eight
  pixels written four bytes at a time did the rest (28 ms). The 50 ms delay is
  overridden to 10 ms: 12.6 fps became 16.2.
- Boing was dropped after Rod

179	  the rotation after Rod saw it, twice (issue #73; its source, notices row and a
180	  `failed_ports.txt` entry stay). `hypnowheel_single_gl.c` registers it only
181	  with `-DHYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`, as the last entry, for measuring. A board profile
182	  showed about 275 ms of its 706 ms step was `double` trig in every vertex, not
183	  fill as first thought; single precision gives 2.2 fps. The rest is fill
184	  (about 334 ms): `-DHYPNOWHEEL_HALF` renders at half resolution
185	  (`glshim_set_render_scale`) for 4.0 fps, still too slow for Rod.
186	- CWaves (`cwaves_single.c`) fills 233 columns, each a 2 by 466 rectangle, so
187	  every store lands on a different cache line of the PSRAM canvas: after single
188	  precision took the step from 95 to 61 ms, 57 of those were the fills and 4
189	  the cosines. The picture depends on x alone, so the wrapper writes each
190	  full-height column into canvas row 0 and the draw wrapper copies that row
191	  down (frames identical to the unmodified hack): 16 ms, 20 fps. Any hack that
192	  paints thin full-height strips can do the same.
193	- A single-precision wrapper must watch for a hack that passes the address of
194	  one of its own `double` locals to a shim function (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &fgs,
195	  &fgv)` in Moire): the prototype still says `double *`, so the float local is
196	  written eight bytes and the frames come out as colour noise, with no
197	  compiler warning. `moire_single.c` defines an adapter before
198	  `single_precision.h` and maps the name to it. Compare the wrapper's frames
199	  with the unmodified hack's: they were all different here, and identical once
200	  the adapter was in. A hack with no decimal literals (Moire) must not be in
201	  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses a file without any.
202	- Moire and Cynosure are paced by their own delays (Moire draws a 20-row chunk
203	  every 50 ms and holds each picture 5 s; Cynosure waits 500 ms a frame, which
204	  is upstream's default), so their fps is low whatever the step is. Cynosure's
205	  `XCreateBitmapFromData`, which the scorer lists as a gap, is inside a
206	  `DO_STIPPLE` block that is never defined.
207	- Moire2 (`moire2_direct.c`, `moire2_planes.h`, built on Halo's planes) keeps
208	  its four depth-1 pixmaps as bit planes and adds an outline circle, an XOR
209	  rectangle, an OR/XOR/copy between planes (the GC's `function`, which the shim
210	  now remembers) and a faster expansion to the window. Upstream's free leaves
211	  its pixmaps to the X server, and the runner frees only the shim's own, so the
212	  wrapper frees the planes. The first version ran at 9.6 fps: the plane copy
213	  and the expansion were 26 and 27 ms, because 64-bit index maths is several
214	  instructions an operation on a 32-bit core and the expansion branched on
215	  every pixel. After clipping everything fits an int; a byte table of eight
216	  pixels written four bytes at a time did the rest (28 ms). The 50 ms delay is
217	  overridden to 10 ms: 12.6 fps became 16.2.
218	- Boing was dropped after Rod saw it (too slow, and plain on a small screen);
219	  its source, notices row and `boing_gl.c` stay, the wrapper out of the build
220	  filter. Its 208 scanlines are blended full-width lines and cost half its
221	  step: 5.0 fps with them, 8.3 without; the ball size barely matters (0.3
222	  saves 13 ms). HexTrail (`hextrail_single_gl.c`) draws
223	  every hexagon it has built, so its step climbs from about 19 ms to a ceiling
224	  and it restarts: use a mean over a cycle (150 s). The grid is `count * 2`
225	  squared, and a smaller count makes fewer, larger hexagons over the same area:
226	  mean 5.7 fps at upstream's 20, 9.1 at 10, 12.7 at 6 (registered,
227	  `-DHEXTRAIL_COUNT=<n>`). Rod found 12.7 too slow once the picture filled
228	  (under 10 fps). Single precision gave 13.0; skipping the depth clear it
229	  never needs (see `gl.md`) gave 15.3, worst window 10.8. The single-precision
230	  wrapper adapts `get_position` and `get_rotation`: the hack passes `double`
231	  locals' addresses, which a float rename would write eight bytes (as Moire).
232	- Celtic (`celtic_single.c`, issue #37) is registered after HexTrail and takes
233	  a median step of 32 ms against 832 as copied (`assessment_measured.md`).
234	  The wrapper is single precision (`rint` and `floor` mapped to float: the
235	  header maps only some libm calls) and frees the colour table that
236	  `celtic_init` callocs. `tools/celtic_patch.py` does three things at build
237	  time. It works `t*n - floor(t*n)` out once and clamps it: in float a fused
238	  multiply-add made it slightly negative and the hack's `assert()` aborted
239	  (the 3000-frame test found it). It sizes the graph to the screen: upstream's
240	  margins of -600 to -900 left most of a pattern off the screen, one held 1.1
241	  MB on the host, and 44 of 300 random starts needed more than the board's free
242	  heap by a model; grid and Kennicott now use minus one edge, and the triangle
243	  width/2 plus two edges (its incircle is half its circumradius). And it
244	  scales the 0.0001 animation tick by `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE` (default 4,
245	  `-DCELTIC_STEP_SCALE=<n>`), which cuts the shadow look-ahead's work and a
246	  picture's draw calls to 100 / scale. A test bounds a pattern's host bytes
247	  over 150 starts. Do not shorten `*delay2`: it is a 5 s dwell on the finished
248	  picture upstream. It looked like a pause on black while the shim's
249	  `erase_window` cleared first (issue #86); now the first call leaves the
250	  picture up and the wipe follows the wait. When forcing a graph type in a
251	  scratch copy to compare, set the margin for that type too, or the triangle
252	  comes out too small to fill the screen.

255	  - "firmware/src/x11shim/**"
256	  - "firmware/src/hacks/registry.*"
257	  - "firmware/src/hacks/*_single.c"
258	  - "firmware/src/hacks/single_precision.h"
259	  - "firmware/platformio.ini"

263	
264	# X11 shim and framework gotchas
265	
266	Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.
267	
268	- `unsigned long` is 4 bytes on the device and 8 on the host, so a hack that
269	  allocates arrays of it (Substrate's two 466 by 466 buffers) is twice the size
270	  on the host, and host leak numbers are twice the device's. On the device,
271	  plain `malloc`/`realloc` of about 868 KB reached PSRAM (free PSRAM fell by
272	  1.74 MB) and came back on restart; internal heap barely moved.
273	- The board's `malloc` is `CONFIG_SPIRAM_USE_MALLOC=y` with
274	  `SPIRAM_MALLOC_ALWAYSINTERNAL=4096`: a block up to 4 KB comes from internal
275	  RAM and falls back to PSRAM when that is full, and a bigger one goes to PSRAM
276	  first. An allocation fails only when PSRAM is gone, so a hack's `abort()` on
277	  a failed allocation is not the risk it looks. The cost of a big pattern is
278	  internal heap drained to near zero (Celtic read 1,792 B free) and its data
279	  in slower PSRAM: compare the log's `psram=` with its idle value for the
280	  overflow.
281	- `erase_window` (`erase.c`) follows upstream's contract: the first call draws
282	  nothing and returns a state, so a hack that waits after it (Celtic's 5 s
283	  `*delay2`) waits on the finished picture. The second call starts a one-second
284	  wipe (blinds, circle, fizzle or random lines, picked at random), each later
285	  call draws the next step, and the call after the second is up clears the
286	  window and returns NULL. Progress comes from `double_time()`, not from the
287	  call count, so the wipe lasts a second at any step rate. A test or tool
288	  that does not sleep for a hack's delay must install a clock
289	  (`xshim_set_clock`), or a wipe never ends. Six hacks never call
290	  `eraser_free`, so the display tracks live states and the runner releases
291	  them when a hack stops.
292	- xlockmore hacks (the 40 that include `xlockmore.h`) need `-DSTANDALONE`,
293	  which every PlatformIO env and `score_hacks.py` set; without it they
294	  include `xlock.h` instead. The envs also define `HAVE_MOBILE`, because
295	  otherwise each hack's `XSCREENSAVER_LINK` defines the same global
296	  `xscreensaver_function_table` and two hacks fail to link; the only other
297	  effect is an inert `*ignoreRotation: True` default. Register one in
298	  `hacks/registry.c` with `XLOCKMORE_HACK(<name>, "<Class>")`. The runner runs
299	  the hack's `setup_cb` once and passes `setup_arg` as `init_cb`'s hidden third
300	  argument, as xscreensaver's `screenhack.c` does. Its table is empty until
301	  then. Resources the framework reads but a hack does not define
302	  (`delta3d`, `size`, ...) fall back to `kFrameworkDefaults` in
303	  `x11shim/resources.c`. A `HackEntry`'s `overrides` list beats the hack's own
304	  defaults (Galaxy runs with `count: -3`, at most three galaxies; a count of
305	  -2 or above skips the hack's restart cleanup and leaks); register it with
306	  `XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH`. Galaxy, Drift, Discrete and Flame are built through
307	  `hacks/<name>_single.c`, which includes the framework headers, then
308	  `hacks/single_precision.h` (`double` and the libm calls become `float` and
309	  the `f` versions; the S3's FPU is single-precision only), then the unmodified
310	  hack; the original `.c` is excluded from each env's `build_src_filter`.
311	- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1), arcs and pixmap writes live in
312	  `x11shim/stroke.c`, `arc.c` and `pixmap.c`. Width 0 and 1 keep the old
313	  `canvas_line` path, so hacks that set no wide width are pixel-identical (every
314	  hack's frame is pinned in `test_hacks.c`). Braid is the one registered hack
315	  that draws wide lines (random width 1-7; Maze's width 2 is under
316	  `HAVE_JWXYZ`). A round-capped segment draws a disc at each end, so
317	  `stroke.c` keeps each width's rows in a table (widths to 16) rather than
318	  calling `canvas_fill_ellipse`, whose `double` maths is software on the S3. A
319	  test pins the pixels to `canvas_fill_ellipse`.
320	- `single_precision.h` renames the keyword `double`, not literals: `0.5 * x`
321	  is still software double. Braid's wrapper includes a copy of the hack with
322	  every decimal literal suffixed `f`, written at build time by
323	  `firmware/patch_float_literals.py` (`tools/float_literals.py`). Check a
324	  wrapper's object for `__muldf3` and friends with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm`.
325	  The older wrappers (Galaxy, Drift, Discrete, Flame, Substrate) have not been
326	  checked.
327	- A colour pixmap is a `Canvas`, and every drawing primitive draws on the
328	  drawable it is given (`xshim_target` in `pixmap.c`); a bitmap or `None`
329	  draws nothing, and only `XCopyArea` writes into a bitmap (`XCopyPlane`
330	  follows the same rule). One exception still draws on the window whatever
331	  it is given: Deluxe's wrapper, which calls `stroke_circle(dpy->canvas,
332	  ...)`. No
333	  registered hack drew into a pixmap before this (the `HAVE_JWXYZ` wrappers
334	  and Deluxe's `doubleBuffer: False` turn double-buffering off), so keep
335	  those: a back buffer costs 434 KB and a full-frame copy, and dirties every
336	  row. Without a
337	  clip mask, `XCopyArea` copies colour rows whole with `canvas_paste_rect`. A
338	  pixmap wider or taller than `INT16_MAX` is `None` (the canvas's dirty spans
339	  are `int16_t`). Truchet draws into one (issue #61). The display tracks every
340	  pixmap a hack holds and the runner frees what a stopped hack left behind
341	  (Pacman leaked 514 KB per start). The GC keeps its own copy of a clip mask
342	  because hacks free the pixmap right after `XSetClipMask`. There is no PNG
343	  decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads
344	  the raw blob described in `ximage-loader.h`, made by
345	  `tools/make_logo_blob.py` (`uv run`, needs Pillow). The `logo_180`/`360`
346	  headers are aliases of the 50 px data, as a 466 px screen only picks 50.
347	  `XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repo root) swaps the logo for a local
348	  image, shrunk to fit 50 px, without committing it: `firmware/logo_override.py`
349	  writes the header into the build dir, where `maze_patched.c` finds it
350	  before the committed one. Unset, it deletes that header. Needs `uv`. A
351	  third-party logo kept under `vendor/` stays out of git that way. The WorkOS
352	  icon is `vendor/workos/workos-icon-256.png`. A plain flash with it is
353	  `unset PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` then `XS_LOGO=vendor/workos/workos-icon-256.png
354	  pio run -e stopwatch -t upload`: build flags stick, so a leftover pin from
355	  an earlier probe would survive. The logo shows in Maze only.
356	- A wide circle through `XDrawArc` is a polyline of about a thousand wide
357	  segments, each filled a row at a time: 40 times the fills of a ring, and the
358	  polyline leaves gaps in it. `stroke_circle` (`x11shim/stroke.c`) fills the
359	  ring in two spans a row. Only Deluxe's wrapper calls it, and it does full
360	  circles only: Pacman's wall arcs are quarters and Celtic's wide strokes are
361	  lines, so they still take the stroker. The polyline's gaps were float
362	  rounding, not the joins or the point spacing: a pixel centre exactly on an
363	  edge shared by a segment quad and the join wedge at its end (any 45 degree
364	  edge through integer vertices) fell out of both, because float32 put the
365	  quad's right edge at 57.499996 for 57.5. `fill_convex` now takes a right
366	  edge inclusive to within `EDGE_SLACK` (1e-3; 1e-7 fails the test, 1e-5
367	  passes), and `test_wide_full_arc_fills_every_pixel_in_its_band` pins it. It
368	  moved five pinned frames by 0 to 33 pixels each (Deluxe, Forest, Rotor,
369	  Compass, Celtic). Pacman is not affected: its `wallwidth` is 1 at this
370	  size, which takes the thin-line path. Celtic's overpaint (about 50 paints a
371	  pixel a step on the host, 46% of its line draws zero-length) is still open
372	  in #56. Changing shared stroke code can move pinned frames: look at them and
373	  ask Rod. The pin test hashes steps 50, 100, 150 and 200 with a fake clock
374	  that carries across hacks, so a dump program does not reproduce its frames:
375	  write them from the test itself.
376	- `XshimGC.alpha` (0 is opaque, 1 to 31 is the weight out of 32) makes the
377	  wide-line code in `stroke.c` blend over the canvas instead of overwriting it;
378	  fills, `canvas_line` and the other primitives ignore it. The canvas is
379	  byte-swapped RGB565, so the blend swaps each pixel and back. A shape of
380	  overlapping pieces (a polyline, a round cap and its segment) sets bits in a
381	  mask the size of the canvas (a 27 KB `calloc` per shape, freed at the end)
382	  and blends it once, or the overlaps blend twice and a star's corners show
383	  as bright diamonds. A failed `calloc` falls back to blending piece by piece.
384	  Setting `alpha` takes a wrapper, as in `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`.
385	- Don't declare `xrealloc` or `xmalloc` in the shim: cloudlife defines its own
386	  static `xrealloc`, which would clash.
387	- `XGetImage` and `XPutImage` (`ximage.c`) move 32-bit ZPixmap images (the raw
388	  RGB565 value in each) to and from the window or a colour pixmap; a bitmap
389	  format, `None` or an empty region gives NULL. XMatrix flips its glyph sheets
390	  through them. Overrunning a row's right edge wraps onto the next row without
391	  AddressSanitizer seeing it, so a clip test must look at that next row.
392	- `XPutImage` copies a 16-bit image a row at a time with `memcpy`; other
393	  depths keep the per-pixel loop, since they keep only the low 16 bits (#82).
394	  ad-flyingtoasters at 2x: step 29.3 to 6.7 ms, 22.3 to 28.5 fps; at 1x: step
395	  15.9 to 3.7 ms. Fireworkx draws its own squares and did not change.
396	- `image_data_to_pixmap` accepts a NULL width, height or mask pointer (XMatrix
397	  passes no mask, and a NULL mask used to crash it on start); with no mask
398	  pointer no mask is made.
399	- `XClearWindow` clears to the colour `XSetWindowBackground` last set
400	  (default 0), and `xshim_release_pixmaps` resets it when a hack stops: the
401	  display outlives the hack, and Hexadrop's colour once turned Pyro's clear
402	  into a solid fill. No key events ever arrive, so `XLookupString` finds no
403	  characters, and an Xt timer (`X11/Intrinsic.h`) is never made.
404	- The shim still draws nothing into a depth-1 pixmap and draws every GC as
405	  `GXcopy`; it only remembers the function in `gc->function` now (GXcopy, GXor,
406	  GXxor). Halo and Moire2 handle both inside their own wrappers
407	  (`halo_planes.h`, `moire2_planes.h`).
408	- `screenhack.h`'s `frand` has a `1.0` inside its macro body, so the float
409	  literal pass cannot reach it and a single-precision wrapper still divides in
410	  double (software on the S3; `nm` shows `__divdf3`). `hacks/single_frand.h`
411	  redefines it in float; it is opt-in, because the older wrappers' frame hashes
412	  are pinned with the original.
413	- Added for the second batch, each test-first: 16-bit ZPixmap `XImage`s
414	  (canvas-order pixels, like every other value the shim hands out: `XAllocColor`
415	  -> `XPutPixel` -> `XPutImage` keeps the pixel; `XPutImage` does not swap.
416	  Only `lowrez_put_image` swaps, because Fireworkx writes ordinary RGB565
417	  bytes straight into the image data) and
418	  `ImageByteOrder`; `CoordModePrevious` in `XFillPolygon`, `XDrawLines` and
419	  `XDrawPoints`; `XCreatePixmapFromBitmapData` (X bitmap data is least
420	  significant bit first); a spline of our own (`spline.c`, not xscreensaver's);
421	  `XQueryColor`; `DisplayOfScreen` (the display opened last); the fill-rule,
422	  fill-style and stipple constants (accepted, ignored: fills are solid and
423	  even-odd); and `XSetFunction` and `jwxyz_XSetAlphaAllowed` (no-ops).
424	- Added for the third batch, each test-first: `ya_random` (the C library's
425	  `random()`, so `ya_rand_init` seeds it); `make_color_ramp` (the short way
426	  round the hue wheel, there and back when `closed_p`; ours, not
427	  xscreensaver's); `visual_depth` (always 16); `xshm.h` with
428	  `create_xshm_image`, `put_xshm_image` and `destroy_xshm_image`, which are a
429	  zeroed 16-bit `XImage` and `XPutImage` (`x11shim/xshm.c`); the arrow and page
430	  keysym constants (X's values; no key event ever arrives); and `glOrtho` (see
431	  `gl.md`). The Edit tool drops a trailing space from `old_string` and
432	  `new_string`: an edit that ends at a space in `platformio.ini`'s
433	  `build_src_filter` glued two entries together (it still built, which hid it).
434	- `allocate_alpha_colors` still finds no colour planes, so a hack that wants
435	  transparency (Qix, Goop) falls back to opaque layers and prints "couldn't
436	  allocate any color planes" on the host.
437	- The comment in `xshim.h` saying `XPutImage` byte-swaps a 16-bit image has
438	  been stale since commit 272ad6a: an `XImage` holds canvas-order pixels. A
439	  hack that builds its own 16-bit image must `px_swap` its pixels first.

---

  - "firmware/pacman_sprites.py"

# Per-hack gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- Maze keeps a 1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one
  `calloc` (about 20 MB; the board has 8 MB of PSRAM). `hacks/maze/maze.c`
  stays byte-identical: `firmware/patch_maze.py` (a PlatformIO `pre:` script
  in every env) writes a copy with both limits at 80 into the build dir, using
  `tools/maze_patch.py`, which fails loudly if upstream's `#define`s change.
  `hacks/maze_small.c` includes that copy and the original is excluded from
  `build_src_filter`. A `gridSize` below 7 would overflow the 80 by 80 arrays.
- Pacman has two build-time patches (`tools/pacman_patch.py`, run by
  `firmware/patch_pacman.py`; wrappers `hacks/pacman_stdlevel.c` and
  `hacks/pacman_loop_ai.c`): the random level generator recursed to ~315 KB
  and boot-looped the board, so a generated level is a copy from
  `hacks/pacman_pool.h` (24 levels, made on the host by
  `tools/pacman_levels.py` with the cells outside the round display walled
  off; the fixed level is still half of them), and the ghosts' route search is
  a loop (it was 453 levels deep). Re-run the tool after changing its mask or
  the generator's tile data. Each patch checks what it replaces. The two host
  pins that follow the game (`kBaseline`'s Pacman and the ghost-route chain)
  depend on how many `random()` values the level pick takes: re-take the chain
  with `pacman_loop_ai.c` temporarily including `pacman/pacman_ai.c`, then
  restore it and check the loop gives the same value. Its sprite sheet is
  built from `vendor/` into the build dir by `firmware/pacman_sprites.py` and
  never committed (3 MB as C text).
- Braid runs at 3-9 fps (0.8-2 before four rounds of work): it redraws every
  segment of the braid each frame to spin the colours. A host profile put its
  disc fill at 6% and the board spent most of its time there, because the Mac
  does `double` at full speed. Split a slow hack's step on the device with a
  temporary flag that returns early from the expensive call.
- Maze fills the whole 466 by 466 square, so its corners and the exit marker
  fall outside the round display's visible circle.
- `check_notices.py` reads 100 lines of header: Maze's licence follows a long
  modification history.
- A hack can be freed before its first draw: two quick presses, or a press
  with the 90 s rotation. `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame`
  runs every hack through it. Blaster's free dereferenced NULL (it sizes a loop
  in init but allocates in draw), so `hacks/blaster_safe.c` includes the
  unmodified hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with a
  free that zeroes `NUM_ROBOTS` when `robots` is NULL.
- Deluxe is built through `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`, which includes the unmodified
  hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with overrides:
  `*transparent: False` (upstream's plane masks need colour planes, which
  `allocate_alpha_colors` reports none of) and `*doubleBuffer: False` (it was
  added when the shim drew only on the canvas, so the `XCopyArea` from its
  blank pixmap erased the picture; pixmaps work now, but two 434 KB back
  buffers and a full-frame copy each frame would cost more than they give).
  The wrapper then gives each throbber's GC an alpha of 26
  of 32 (upstream's translucent weight) and sends full wide circles to
  `stroke_circle`. A plain screenhack's `HackEntry` has no overrides unless a
  wrapper builds it. Its step is 45-63 ms on the device against a 32.5 ms push,
  so about 11-13 fps; ideas for more are in issue #54.
- Eight of the S-hack batch (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes,
  Halftone, Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole) are built through
  `hacks/<name>_direct.c` (pixmap double buffering, see `techniques.md`;
  LMorph's is `lmorph_single.c` because it needs no `HAVE_JWXYZ`). All but
  Anemotaxis and Wormhole, and Euler2D (`euler2d_single.c`), also use
  `single_precision.h` plus build-time float literals (`patch_float_literals.py`
  lists them). `single_precision.h` leaves `floor` and `ceil` on the double
  versions: Euler2D's wrapper maps them itself. After the literal pass, `nm`
  still shows soft-double helpers in Euler2D, Halftone, Interaggregate and
  Anemone; their source was not chased.
- `test_frames_of_every_hack_but_maze_match_main` stops at the first hash that
  differs, in registry order, so repinning several hacks takes one test run
  each (about 85 s), earliest first. A hack whose frames do not change under a
  wrapper (Compass and Halftone in single precision) keeps its hash.
- Anemone's step moves between 31 and 56 ms as its arms grow and shrink, so its
  fps is 11 to 15.5 whatever one 20 s window says. Forest waits 500 ms between
  trees by design (about 2 fps, and the push is 88 rows).
- A hack that unpacks pixel values itself (Substrate and Interaggregate, in
  their `point2rgb`) assumes ordinary RGB565, but the canvas holds the bytes
  swapped. Its wrapper swaps pixels where they cross `XAllocColor` and
  `XSetForeground`. Interaggregate shipped without this: its alpha blends
  mixed the wrong bit fields and drew rainbow noise instead of green and brown
  strokes. `test_interaggregate_blend` includes the wrapper to check one blend.
- `dump` never seeds `random()`, so a hack that picks a mode at start (Truchet,
  12 modes) shows the same one in every dump. To see others, build the hack
  alone (`probe_hacks.registry_source` and `shim_sources`) from a copy outside
  `vendor/`, with a `__attribute__((constructor))` that calls

  into the PSRAM canvas a frame. Single precision, a float convex fill and
  two-pixel stores took it from 2.4 to 10.2 fps with pixel-identical frames.

- XMatrix needs `matrix_glyphs.py` (a `pre:` script in every env), which

  `textclient.h` stand-in never opens a source, and Xt timers never fire.
- Flurry is not ported. It draws 3,600 blended, textured quads a frame and
  needs `glAlphaFunc`, `glRectd`, `gluBuild2DMipmaps` and luminance-alpha
  textures, none in TinyGL here. With `gl_budget.py`'s per-vertex and
  per-pixel costs that is well under 1 fps (arithmetic, not a measurement:
  the tool cannot read a multi-file hack).
- Qix and Fireworkx both leaked on every stop, found by the restart leak test.
  Qix's `qix_free` skips each segment's `lines[i].p` array (about 48 KB per
  stop); Fireworkx below 24 bits never frees its own 565 image buffer (48 KB).
  Their wrappers (`qix_direct.c`, `fireworkx_single.c`) free the missing piece
  before calling upstream's free. LeakSanitizer does not run on macOS, but
  `MallocStackLogging=1 leaks --atExit -- .pio/build/dump/program <index> 0

  `pio test` deletes the program).
- Starfish and Goop spent most of a frame in the shim's polygon fill (double
  maths per edge per row). `hacks/float_polygon.h` fills any even-odd polygon
  in float, optionally mixed in at an alpha in 32nds (all three colour
  channels with one multiply), and took Starfish from 8.5 to 19 fps. Goop draws
  straight onto the window (its `XCreatePixmap` is the window and the
  `XCopyArea` is skipped) and blends each blob in at the alpha upstream's jwxyz
  path uses. Its full-frame clear cost 15 ms, so `hacks/span_erase.h` erases
  only the bounding boxes the blobs filled last frame (pixel-identical frames):
  14.6-15.2 fps translucent. The shared `canvas_fill_polygon` is still double
  (Hexadrop has its own convex float fill). Goop is built through
  `goop_direct.c` with `HAVE_JWXYZ`; the colour-plane path needs planes the
  canvas lacks.
- A wrapper that does `#define double float` must include any header with a
  `double` in a struct the shim's `.c` files also use BEFORE the define: the
  hack includes it again, the guard keeps the copy seen through the macro, and
  the two sides disagree on the layout. `spline.h` did this to Starfish and
  Goop: they drew garbage (flat colours) at 16-20 fps and their first pinned
  hashes were of it. Look at a frame after any change that is not
  pixel-identical by construction;
  `test_hacks_that_use_the_spline_draw_a_real_picture` now fails on a flat
  screen.
- Fireworkx renders at 1/`FIREWORKX_SCALE` of the width and height
  (`hacks/lowrez_put.h`: it is told the window is smaller and `XPutImage`
  draws each pixel as a square): 2.4 fps as copied, 11 at a scale of 3, 12.4 at
  4. Its glow, flash pass and 565 conversion are full-frame walks over PSRAM.
  Its header says "(GPL)" but the text is the standard permission notice.
  Everything it works in is in pixels, tuned for a window about 1024 wide: at
  152 pixels a burst filled the picture and the glow blur (energy kept, output
  doubled) saturated, so the screen was white. `tools/fireworkx_patch.py`
  (run before the float literal pass; the copy stays byte-identical) scales the
  spark speed, gravity, flash reach and velocity jitter by the render width
  over 1024, and the wrapper throws 120 sparks a shell instead of 500 and fires
  two of its four shells. 12.4-12.6 fps, with a dark background between
  bursts. The shell count cannot change (it is baked into the SSE layout), so
  the idle shells are given an endless life and no sparks.
- Loop asks for 100 ms between generations (8.7 fps with a 3.5-7 ms step); the
  registry overrides it to 50 ms. It also took `malloc(0)` returning NULL, which
  the board does and the host does not, for out of memory: square mode asks
  for a rectangle list for each of eight colour states, most empty, and it
  freed its cells and drew nothing more (a black screen at 18 fps, half the
  starts, never seen on the host). `loop_direct.c` asks for one byte, and a test
  swaps in an allocator that returns NULL for zero. Hypnowheel was dropped from
  the rotation after Rod saw it, twice (issue #73; its source, notices row and a
  `failed_ports.txt` entry stay). `hypnowheel_single_gl.c` registers it only
  with `-DHYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`, as the last entry, for measuring. A board profile
  showed about 275 ms of its 706 ms step was `double` trig in every vertex, not
  fill as first thought; single precision gives 2.2 fps. The rest is fill
  (about 334 ms): `-DHYPNOWHEEL_HALF` renders at half resolution
  (`glshim_set_render_scale`) for 4.0 fps, still too slow for Rod.
- CWaves (`cwaves_single.c`) fills 233 columns, each a 2 by 466 rectangle, so
  every store lands on a different cache line of the PSRAM canvas: after single
  precision took the step from 95 to 61 ms, 57 of those were the fills and 4
  the cosines. The picture depends on x alone, so the wrapper writes each
  full-height column into canvas row 0 and the draw wrapper copies that row
  down (frames identical to the unmodified hack): 16 ms, 20 fps. Any hack that
  paints thin full-height strips can do the same.
- A single-precision wrapper must watch for a hack that passes the address of
  one of its own `double` locals to a shim function (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &fgs,
  &fgv)` in Moire): the prototype still says `double *`, so the float local is
  written eight bytes and the frames come out as colour noise, with no
  compiler warning. `moire_single.c` defines an adapter before
  `single_precision.h` and maps the name to it. Compare the wrapper's frames
  with the unmodified hack's: they were all different here, and identical once
  the adapter was in. A hack with no decimal literals (Moire) must not be in
  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses a file without any.
- Moire and Cynosure are paced by their own delays (Moire draws a 20-row chunk
  every 50 ms and holds each picture 5 s; Cynosure waits 500 ms a frame, which
  is upstream's default), so their fps is low whatever the step is. Cynosure's
  `XCreateBitmapFromData`, which the scorer lists as a gap, is inside a
  `DO_STIPPLE` block that is never defined.
- Moire2 (`moire2_direct.c`, `moire2_planes.h`, built on Halo's planes) keeps
  its four depth-1 pixmaps as bit planes and adds an outline circle, an XOR
  rectangle, an OR/XOR/copy between planes (the GC's `function`, which the shim
  now remembers) and a faster expansion to the window. Upstream's free leaves
  its pixmaps to the X server, and the runner frees only the shim's own, so the
  wrapper frees the planes. The first version ran at 9.6 fps: the plane copy
  and the expansion were 26 and 27 ms, because 64-bit index maths is several
  instructions an operation on a 32-bit core and the expansion branched on
  every pixel. After clipping everything fits an int; a byte table of eight
  pixels written four bytes at a time did the rest (28 ms). The 50 ms delay is
  overridden to 10 ms: 12.6 fps became 16.2.
- Boing was dropped after Rod saw it (too slow, and plain on a small screen);
  its source, notices row and `boing_gl.c` stay, the wrapper out of the build
  filter. Its 208 scanlines are blended full-width lines and cost half its

  every hexagon it has built, so its step climbs from about 19 ms to a ceiling
  and it restarts: use a mean over a cycle (150 s). The grid is `count * 2`
  squared, and a smaller count makes fewer, larger hexagons over the same area:
  mean 5.7 fps at upstream's 20, 9.1 at 10, 12.7 at 6 (registered,
  `-DHEXTRAIL_COUNT=<n>`). Rod found 12.7 too slow once the picture filled
  (under 10 fps). Single precision gave 13.0; skipping the depth clear it
  never needs (see `gl.md`) gave 15.3, worst window 10.8. The single-precision
  wrapper adapts `get_position` and `get_rotation`: the hack passes `double`
  locals' addresses, which a float rename would write eight bytes (as Moire).
- Celtic (`celtic_single.c`, issue #37) is registered after HexTrail and takes
  a median step of 32 ms against 832 as copied (`assessment_measured.md`).
  The wrapper is single precision (`rint` and `floor` mapped to float: the
  header maps only some libm calls) and frees the colour table that
  `celtic_init` callocs. `tools/celtic_patch.py` does three things at build
  time. It works `t*n - floor(t*n)` out once and clamps it: in float a fused
  multiply-add made it slightly negative and the hack's `assert()` aborted

  margins of -600 to -900 left most of a pattern off the screen, one held 1.1

  heap by a model; grid and Kennicott now use minus one edge, and the triangle
  width/2 plus two edges (its incircle is half its circumradius). And it

  picture's draw calls to 100 / scale. A test bounds a pattern's host bytes

  picture upstream. It looked like a pause on black while the shim's
  `erase_window` cleared first (issue #86); now the first call leaves the
  picture up and the wipe follows the wait. When forcing a graph type in a
  scratch copy to compare, set the margin for that type too, or the triangle
  comes out too small to fill the screen.
